description: We are a team passionate about space exploration and technology, participating in the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our goal is to build a simple and interactive web application to explore SPHEREx sky images and observe changes over time. We welcome members interested in astrophysics, web development, data analysis, visualization, and AI/ML.
summary:
SPHEREx & Planet X | Sky Discovery Lab is an interactive web application developed by Team madeo publico to make NASA's infrared sky observations accessible to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts.

Our platform connects to NASA's SPHEREx archive through Caltech/IPAC IRSA, allowing users to search celestial coordinates, explore real astronomical observations, and visualize scientific FITS images directly in their browsers. Users can examine observation dates, infrared wavelength information, and original data sources through an accessible interface.

To support the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we developed a time-comparison workflow that evaluates image quality, wavelength compatibility, and sky-coordinate alignment before allowing observations from different periods to be compared. The application also includes image visualization controls and investigation tools for documenting potential changes.

Our Planet X Lab helps users understand how repeated observations can support investigations of distant moving objects while distinguishing possible changes from noise and instrumental effects. It does not claim to have discovered Planet X.

By combining real NASA data, scientific validation, and intuitive visualization, our project makes exploring the changing universe more accessible and educational.
details:
SPHEREx & Planet X | Sky Discovery Lab is a web application developed by team madeo publico to help people explore genuine SPHEREx infrared observations and understand how observations taken at different times can support moving-object investigations.

The application brings together three connected workspaces: Sky Explorer, Time Comparison, and Planet X Lab.

What it does and how it works

Sky Explorer connects to the Caltech/IPAC IRSA archive to search SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 observation metadata, with optional deep-field searches. Users can enter celestial coordinates, resolve an astronomical target name, or choose a preset region. The application downloads small FITS cutouts on demand and generates browser-compatible previews. Observation identifiers, timestamps, and archive links help users trace each image to its source.

Time Comparison performs a bounded search for promising observation pairs. Before displaying an aligned comparison, the backend checks observation times, shared sky coverage, quality masks, valid science pixels, and local wavelength compatibility. Accepted images are resampled onto a common celestial coordinate grid and displayed with shared intensity scaling. Side-by-side views, a before-and-after slider, and adjustable blink playback allow users to inspect two genuine epochs. The application does not generate intermediate observations.

Planet X Lab provides an educational investigation workspace with a checklist, candidate notes, and JSON export of observation metadata and provenance. It encourages users to consider alternative explanations for apparent changes, including noise, instrumental artifacts, and differences in image properties.

Benefits and intended impact

Our aim is to lower the technical barrier to exploring astronomical archive data. Students, educators, and space enthusiasts can inspect real observations without manually processing FITS files or writing analysis scripts.

The project connects curiosity about Planet X with the practical steps of evidence-based investigation: comparing observations, checking data quality, documenting uncertainty, and preserving sources. It supports learning and preliminary visual exploration; it does not automatically detect moving objects or confirm a Planet X discovery.

Tools and technologies

The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The backend uses Python and FastAPI. Astropy handles FITS files, observation times, and coordinate transformations; NumPy supports array processing; Pillow generates image previews; and HTTPX handles archive requests.

SQLite stores observation metadata, while local FITS and PNG caches reduce repeated downloads. Git and GitHub support collaborative development and version control. Browser checks use Playwright.

Creative approach

Our approach combines an accessible visual interface with explicit scientific compatibility checks. Users can move from archive search to image inspection, epoch comparison, and documented investigation within one application.

Rather than presenting every pair as comparable, the application explains rejected comparisons. This makes scientific limitations part of the learning experience and helps users understand why images of the same region may not support a meaningful comparison.

Validation and design considerations

A comparison of genuine cached observations 2025W45_2A_0496_2 and 2025W46_2A_0302_2 passed the implemented checks with 824 shared valid pixels. Their observation times are approximately 6.181 days apart.

Our team considered responsive layouts, readable controls, source attribution, archive outages, download limits, caching, and transparent error messages. Single-observation viewing remains available when a compatible pair cannot be found.

The current comparison uses nearest-neighbor WCS resampling. It does not perform point-spread-function matching or uncertainty-propagated difference photometry. Apparent changes therefore require further scientific analysis and independent observations before being interpreted as physical motion.
